speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We are living in a disruptive world where the pace of change is rapid and relentless.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Faced with unprecedented technological advancements such as generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) and an increasingly complex global order, education must evolve beyond static textbooks and a conventionally didactic model, where there is a one-way transmission of knowledge from teacher to student.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As the Ministry strives towards these goals, I recognise that this work is shared with our educators and school staff, as well as those based in our institutes of continuous learning.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is their dedication that will ensure the success of our endeavours.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am heartened that our students demonstrated strong ability in applying thinking and reasoning processes to solve complex real-world problems, and we must continue to uplift our students with diverse abilities from diverse backgrounds by building on their 21st century competencies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To this end for this year's Committee of Supply (COS) debate, I will focus my speech today on what I call the multi-vitamin strategy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The concept behind the multi-vitamin strategy is simple.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We do not rely on a single vitamin for our health needs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Why then should we expect learners to follow a singular academic path based on the same curriculum?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Therefore, just as a multivitamin supplement provides an assortment of nutrients for overall health from young to old, supporting the holistic development of all students and learners, allow me to elaborate on the ingredients of the multivitamin strategy from vitamins A to K.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our next generation will need to grapple with existential-level challenges such as climate crisis and Singapore's place in an increasingly fragmented and adversarial global environment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They will need to be highly able, agile and adaptable, driven by passion and purpose, agile with the courage to take risks and innovate responsibly, and adaptable to stay resilient amid changes and curveballs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These are tall orders and will require us to provide a wider range of resources and opportunities to every student to maximise their potential.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Vitamin B is to broaden definitions of success by placing greater emphasis on areas such as adaptive and inventive thinking, innovation and civic literacy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This means shifting our educational priorities away from a narrow focus on great performance to valuing the diverse skills and potential of every individual.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This not only honours diversity and strength, and levels the playing field, but is also necessary to meet the demands of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I submit that the academic training and skills acquired should not just lead to jobs, but to marry the passions and interests of our students and learners, so as to maximise each individual's full potential, avoid a mismatch of expectations and minimise involuntarily non-time-based under-employment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The evolving educational landscape demands a focus on cultivating 21st century competencies and skills in today's students and learners across the educational continuum.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Emphasising critical thinking, creativity, collaboration and communication prepares learners for the complexities of a rapidly changing world.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: By integrating technology, tenacity, empathy and resilience into curricula from early childhood to higher education, students develop a holistic skill set essential for success in the digital age.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Nurturing these skills ensures that learners are equipped to navigate challenges, innovate and excel in an ever-evolving global society.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the realm of education in Singapore, dreaming of innovative pedagogies and andragogy, daring to challenge conventional norms and taking proactive steps to implement change to keep pace with the speed of development are key pillars for enhancing the system.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: By encouraging students to dream beyond boundaries, educators can foster creativity and critical thinking.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Daring to introduce novel teaching methods and curriculum adaptations promotes adaptability to societal needs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Ultimately, through a collective commitment to dare to dream, dare to dare and dare to do, Singapore can achieve a dynamic and progressive educational landscape for the future.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Vitamin E – empowering all students and learners.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Vitamin E aims to empower students from diverse backgrounds with diverse learning needs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It acknowledges that there cannot be a one-size-fits-all to learning.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Instead, learning must be customisable, collaborative and with content that is ahead of the curve and speed to market.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I suggest we should examine how much resources we dedicate to those with special needs vis-à-vis our other students and learners.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: One lacuna I observe is when many of these students in the special education (SPED) schools hit 18 years of age and start to experience adult life.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We can and should do more to help empower them, their families and ensure that those with such needs are able to assimilate into the adult life and the future of work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Vitamin K is to keep learning for life.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We do not stop needing essential and necessary nutrients as we age.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In the same vein, adult learners need to embrace continual education and training (CET), even after leaving school to diversify their skills portfolio and career paths amidst a fast-changing and competitive job market.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To better attract adult learners who have to balance their work and caregiving commitments, CET must be well-designed to be effective in improving employment outcomes and made accessible.

speaker: The Chairman
text: I will remember to take all my vitamins this weekend.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To continue with the metaphor, I would like to focus on Vitamin F, which is flexibility.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Subject-based Banding (SBB) is an educational framework implemented in Singapore's secondary school system.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As mentioned, SBB aims at giving students flexibility, for example, to take different subjects at different levels according to their preferences, strengths and interests.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, students may offer a subject at the Express level while taking other subjects at the Normal (Academic) or Normal (Technical) levels, to use previous older terms.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, it also allows for customised learning, so that schools can curate learning experiences to address the needs of different learners with differing needs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our educators can also vary the learning support given and provide differentiated instructions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This helps them ensure that learning addresses students' individual learning profiles.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, the stigma linked previously to streaming can be reduced.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Students, realistically, can do well in the subjects they have a deep interest in, regardless of their overall academic stream.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: SBB also facilitates smoother transitions between different academic levels and is, therefore, far less rigid, allowing for much interaction amongst students of different academic abilities in different subjects.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Overall, Sir, SBB is adaptive and inclusive and puts more emphasis on holistic development.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Chairman, bilingual education is a cornerstone of our education policy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, and in recognition of the status of Tamil as an official Indian mother tongue, MOE ensures that funding for the official mother tongues, namely Malay, Mandarin and Tamil, is higher than that of the five NTILs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Apart from Hindi, the number of students taking the four other non-Tamil mother tongue languages is far smaller.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: All in all, MOE's broad approach towards the various NTILs is inclusive, while acknowledging the position of Tamil as the official Indian mother tongue language.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I also enquire if the Ministry independently assesses the salaries of NTIL teachers and whether they are remunerated reasonably, in view of the important role they play in the Ministry's bilingual language policy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, the parallel programme landscape varies considerably for the NTILs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The parallel programme saves many students a trip to a centralised school over the weekend to learn their NTIL mother tongue, leaving these children with more time to engage in other academic and non-academic pursuits.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I have two other questions in this regard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can I confirm what is MOE's policy towards new requests for parallel programmes by ethnic groups in charge of NTILs with a small enrolment, so that more of our students can be served by them?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One result of this policy is that community groups with smaller NTIL enrolment see it far more economical and logistically convenient to hold weekend classes, even if parallel programmes may be the preference of some parents.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I ask the Government to undertake a review of the NTIL space, with a view to consider the new challenges of community groups, students and parents.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Teaching resources have to be adjusted and devoted to offer students greater flexibility to study more subjects at different levels that suit their interests, aptitudes and learning needs.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: For most schools, they are still operating the previous academic streaming system for the older cohorts.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I understand that full SBB also means staggered recess periods, and different end times for classes which will make planning after-school activities more complicated.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Over the last two months, when full SBB has been implemented at scale, may I ask the Minister what is the experience so far on how the schools and teachers have been coping and adjusting?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: It would be useful for students and parents to understand the operational challenges and work with the schools to reap the full, intended benefits of SBB.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: The SEC will reflect the different subject combinations and levels.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: I would like the MOE to share how the SEC system will affect these national examinations, and how the results will be used for students to choose and be selected for the various post-secondary pathways.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I also mentioned the work of EveryChild.sg, whose White Paper advocates for PSLE to be an optional pathway.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister for Education raised a few issues with a through-train programme.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister said that it is neither realistic nor desirable to shield our children from all stresses.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But we are talking about young children below the age of 13 years.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even adults can have trouble managing stress, what more young children?

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The stress of PSLE is arguably not age-appropriate.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In addition, it does not mean that a child who faces stress from a young age will necessarily grow up to handle stress better as an adult.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, the opposite might be true; a child who faces an unhealthy amount of stress at a young age might develop mental health conditions that continue into adulthood.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is no one school in Singapore that can cater to all learners.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us open up a new range of schools, small and mid-sized, with some offering non-PSLE routes, helmed by progressive school leaders.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe MOE already has school leaders who are ready to pilot a through train.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Let us also allow flexibility for students to switch schools or programmes if they find themselves in one that is unsuitable.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Minister also argued that removing PSLE would deny parents and students the ability to choose their schools.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My answer to that is that our current system denies parents the choice of not letting their children take PSLE.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Parents can make this choice if we pilot the through train.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do not have to choose the popular schools for the through-train pilot.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Those who wish to enter these popular schools can continue to do so through the PSLE route.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If a student mixes with 40 other students every year, he or she will get to meet 400 other students over 10 years.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since the average number of students in each school is about 1,200, this is not a limitation.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, it is the PSLE system that has contributed to stratification when we group students with similar scores together.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As for academic checkpoints, we can and should trust the quality of internal school examinations.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Having a through-train programme does not mean there will be no exams.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If a child wants to transfer to another school, MOE can allow them to use their internal school exam results to do so.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Making PSLE optional would be a game changer.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Families that want the PSLE to add to their children's portfolio can continue with it.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Families which do not, can choose the non-PSLE route and focus their children on other assessments that are benchmarked against real life skills and contexts.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Instead, the primary school outcomes focus on general attributes.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These include pupils being able to distinguish right from wrong, knowing their strengths and areas for growth, having a lively curiosity about their surroundings, taking pride in their work and being able to cooperate, as well as share and care for others.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is therefore much more value to primary schooling than preparation for this major exam."

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Chairman, in the digital age, the integration of technology into education emerges not just as a trend but as a fundamental shift in how knowledge is acquired, processed and applied.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The importance of leveraging technology to enhance education lies in its unparalleled potential to foster more inclusive, engaging and personalised learning experiences.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Through digital tools and platforms, educators can tailor instruction to meet the diverse needs of students, accommodating various learning styles and pace.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Technology facilitates access to a vast repository of information and resources; breaking down geographical and socio-economic barriers to education; encourages interactive learning – where students are not passive recipients of information but active participants in their educational journey; exploring concepts through multimedia content; virtual simulations and global classrooms.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, technology has a crucial place in Singapore's education system, as we strive for academic excellence and innovation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Singapore, the integration of information and communication technology (ICT) in education has been a strategic priority to enhance teaching and learning outcomes.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So far, technology including ICT and AI, are critical to education in Singapore and how it can be used to achieve learning objectives.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Technology allows students to access a vast amount of information and resources beyond what is given in textbooks.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Technology also allows for customisation and for personalised learning so that learning can be driven by individual needs and preferences.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: MOE has been actively promoting the use of technology in through the Masterplan for ICT in Education.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Technology is pivotal to these initiatives to catalyse educational innovation, allow for pedagogical transformation and help to achieve continuous improvement in teaching and learning in Singapore schools and institutions.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Also, Mr Chairman, a key part of learning technology – the devices that will be used to help support learning technology.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will really enhance the learning and development of the younger ones with regard to learning technology.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, given the increasing demand for AI skills in the workforce, it is crucial to help our students develop not just good foundations and fundamental skills but also become proficient in using common AI tools.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For example, all students need to be taught how to correctly input prompts into GenAI tools like ChatGPT to get their desired output.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They also need to be taught how to check for hallucinations, avoid plagiarism and adhere to ethical and legal boundaries so that they can use these technologies safely and responsibly.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I emphasise that this needs to be taught to all students, starting at the primary and early secondary levels and not just those who sign up for AI student outreach programmes or in individual schools on an ad hoc basis.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: More well-resourced families often enrol their children in AI enrichment classes to enhance their digital skills, while lower-income families have less access to them, creating a digital divide across socio-economic groups.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, while AI tools are important, impassionate machines cannot replace an inspirational and empathetic teacher.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, AI tools should always augment, not replace teachers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By doing so, we can combine technology and traditional learning to build a holistic and comprehensive educational experience for each student.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam, please take your two cuts together.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Chairman, the challenges faced by families of children with special needs are multifaceted.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are emotional, financial, logistical and other struggles that families have to deal with on a daily basis.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As a parent of a child with special needs who attends a SPED school, I have had the good fortune of meeting and engaging with different families with similar circumstances.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They have given some meaningful insights which I wish to share.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is important to state at the outset that these families care for their special children deeply and find their journey with the children most rewarding and meaningful.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They would not have it any other way.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, the difficulties are real and the daily grind can get rather overwhelming.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are certain expenses and considerations that these families have to think about that others do not have to.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These may not be the same for all families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Increased cost of living and demands at work exacerbates the situation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I appreciate that there are already subsidies, tax reliefs and other support in place for these families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The funds in the Child Development Account (CDA) could also be used to pay for a wide variety of services, like early intervention programmes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I would appreciate it though if the Government could review the support given.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It would be meaningful if some targeted support could be further extended to alleviate challenges in certain aspects.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For the SPED schools, there may be specific areas to look at.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In recent times, I received feedback on the increased cost of school bus services from a parent with a child in a SPED school.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Another parent who has a child with cerebral palsy had challenges in placing her children in an after-school student care centre.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some parents also lament about the process and time needed to prepare for the application for SPED schools.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Some may not have sufficient information or the bandwidth to sort out the necessary arrangements.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These are some examples of pain points shared.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Has there been an assessment of some of the challenges students of SPED schools and their parents face?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It may be helpful to identify how significant and prevalent the challenges are and what more could be done to assist the families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Reduction of the high costs will meaningfully assist the families, to navigate cost-of-living challenges.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Accessibility to obtain information or services, like after-school care and therapy programmes that could possibly be placed within the school compounds or vicinity, would go a long way is addressing the families' pain points.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Mr Chairman, I have met many educators and officers in the special education sector who are deeply committed to their work.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They have different challenges from their counterparts in mainstream schools and typically have to work with many more students who may be less compliant or on occasion aggressive or deal with family situations that are more complex because of health or care arrangements.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Regardless of the circumstances, these professionals often take this in their stride and go the extra mile to nurture the students under their care.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Because the job can be rather challenging, it would be tough to attract or even retain people in this sector.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Therefore, there should be fair and attractive salaries and career pathways for those in this profession.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The remuneration needs to be commensurate with the demands of the job and there needs to be a stronger effort to entice good people into the sector.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: MOE also shared that key staff and leaders in SPED schools can also look forward to more avenues for professional development, such as opportunities to reinforce teachers' skills in working with students of different disabilities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is very welcomed news as it signals an acknowledgement of the importance of the educators in this sector and will certainly go some way in attracting and retaining talent.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Hopefully, this will create a larger pool of capable educators who can develop deeper skills on more specific issues and enhance the support for our students with special educational needs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Apart from financial incentives, an integral part of the move is the professional development.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As we enhance the pedagogy and curriculum for students in the mainstream schools, we also need to do likewise for students in the SPED schools.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As there are different needs and disabilities, this effort can be a massive task.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We therefore need to ensure that we have skilled educators in the SPED schools.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am supportive of the Ministry's efforts on this front and I look forward to the updates.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Chairman, Sir, I commend MOE for continuing to focus on enhancing its SPED system to better support students with diverse learning needs.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Since 2021, I believe MOE has worked with SPED educators and stakeholders to co-construct SPED Teaching and Learning Syllabuses (TLSs) to raise quality of curriculum, teaching and learning.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: MOE has been providing additional funding, resources and training opportunities for teachers and staff to better understand and address the needs of students with such challenges.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: MOE has also recognised the need for clear career progression pathways for educators in this field.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: This funding is aimed at increasing teacher salaries and expanding professional development opportunities for key staff and leaders with the aim is of attracting and retaining talent as well as optimising the special education system.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Overall, Chairman, Sir, Singapore's recent developments in SPED reflect a commitment to providing inclusive and quality education for students with diverse learning needs – with a focus on supporting their holistic development and preparing them for meaningful participation in society.

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: With that in mind, while we continue to enhance special education and equip SPED students with academic and life-skills, can MOE also do more to work with perhaps MOM and the private sector, to ensure that SPED students are able to secure meaningful employment when they graduate?

speaker: Mr Darryl David
text: Can there also be some continuing education programmes tailored specifically for SPED students to ensure that they stay relevant and employable?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: He mentioned that his per capita income of $1,000 exceeded the qualifying amount by $250.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Mr X is the sole breadwinner, supporting his wife and three children.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: His wife is a homemaker, not by choice, due to the caregiving of their special needs child.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: He lamented that middle-income Singaporeans were being deprived of subsidies that are made available to lower-income groups.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, I do feel that more can be done to help middle-income families with a child who has special needs.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: While the Government considers the Workers' Party proposal towards equalising the fees between SPED schools and the mainstream ones; can it, in the interim, adopt a similarly tiered approach to ensure more equitable outcomes and provide much-needed relief for middle-income families with a special needs child?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, Character and Citizenship Education (CCE) plays a pivotal role in fostering empathy among students.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: However, MOE must ensure that these lessons go beyond theoretical understanding to meaningful interactions.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: An SEN officer cannot always be there to facilitate integration.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It is therefore crucial that all students are aware about disabilities, so they can better support and include their peers.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In my survey, more than a few persons with disabilities (PwDs) also spoke about their hopes for more disability awareness education at mainstream schools.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Could MOE study ways to incorporate more of such lessons into the primary and secondary school curricula?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For example, students can be taught about autism.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This will help them better understand challenges faced by their autistic peers, and know about things like autistic burnouts.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: One point raised in my survey is that teachers can play an active "ice-breaking" role, to help students interact meaningfully with PwDs.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We need to ensure that teachers get all the help that they need, to better perform this role.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, as mentioned in my speech during the Budget debate, I hope MOE can strongly consider proactively including students with disabilities into activities like Physical Education lessons.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, there is a need to further strengthen the educational support for these students.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For students with physical and sensory disabilities, such as the blind, the deaf and those hard of hearing, there is little excuse to not do good by and for them – given the well-established best practices available worldwide.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Today, I will focus on the learning support needed by students, now commonly identified as neurodiverse.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Neurodiversity is an umbrella term used to describe a wide range of differences in the way one thinks and processes information.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), autism, dyslexia, dyspraxia and dyscalculia are some common forms of neurodiversity.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Neurodiverse students often struggle with traditional education systems that fail to meet their unique learning and social needs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: They may be at higher risk of being victimised in schools by bullies.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Those who are from lower-income families often get diagnosed and receive intervention much later, leading to increased vulnerability.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: However, with appropriate training and support, neurodiverse students can offer valuable talents and perspectives in education and work settings.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Chair, we thank all Members for your suggestions, comments on our education system and most importantly, we want to thank you all for the support for our educators.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our education system has done well by most conventional measures.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We continue to surpass ourselves in the PISA rankings.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Our least-privileged students, on average, do better than the Organization of Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) average.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: The vast majority of our graduates find employment quickly, with good starting salaries.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: But we must be careful not to become victims of our own success – chasing yesterday's metrics of success, instead of building the competencies we need for our future.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: We should also be keenly aware that others are catching up and aiming to overtake us with new disruptive technologies and new pedagogies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Many of us worry that the system will only allow us one chance.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: That our futures will somehow, be set in stone if we fail one exam or get into a less popular school or less favoured course.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: When in fact, we have a lifetime ahead of us.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: This chart will illustrate the lifetime investment in our people, today and tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, up to the secondary school level, we invest around $200,000 in every student.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This establishes the strong academic foundations and values for the rest of their lives.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Next, at the post-secondary level, we make another major investment to help our students acquire a work-ready qualification through ITE, polytechnic or university pathways.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Using an ITE student as an example, the subsidy will be around $70,000 for a Nitec and Higher Nitec qualification.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, on average, we would have invested more than a quarter million dollars for every Singaporean child to prepare them for their first career.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As announced in the Budget speech, we will invest more in our ITE graduates through the ITE Progression Award (IPA).

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, as shown in the chart, an ITE graduate who upgrades via a part-time polytechnic diploma will not need to pay any fees out-of-pocket after using the $5,000 top-up.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This can give them a head-start in buying their first home, or saving for retirement.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Some Members have asked, how we are supporting younger working adults?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For those under 40, they are in the earlier stages of their career and their first work-ready qualifications should still serve them well.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But they may need regular, shorter skills top-ups.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For this, they can use the SkillsFuture Credit of $500 that they receive at the age 25 to offset their course fees.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For those aged 40 and above – who have left school for a longer period of time – will require a more substantial skills reboot.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Many in this group recognise the importance of lifelong learning and want to build career resilience through reskilling and upskilling.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, due to financial and other commitments, the course fees and potential loss of income during full-time training can hold them back.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As announced in the Budget speech, we will introduce the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme to support these Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Members have asked for details of the new initiatives.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: How is this different from the existing SkillsFuture Credit of $500?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The $500 credit is meant to cultivate a national culture and broad-based interest in continuous learning.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It can be used for a wide range of skills-related courses, whether you are at the start of your career, mid-way through, or in your silver years.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This $4,000 credit is geared towards boosting employability.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It will not expire, so that you can use it at a juncture that suits you.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The top-up can be used for over 7,000 full-time and part-time courses with better employability outcomes and they will cover academic full qualification programmes offered by our IHLs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: These will include diplomas, post-diplomas, undergraduate and postgraduate degrees that are well-recognised in the market; as well as shorter modules that can stack to these full qualifications, to offer more flexible upgrading options.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And it will also include industry-specific training, such as SkillsFuture Singapore's (SSG's) SkillsFuture Career Transition Programme (SCTP), which is a train-and-place programme that supports individuals moving into sectors with good hiring opportunities; and it will also cover courses that fulfil the training requirements in the Progressive Wage Model sectors, to support the career and wage progression of lower-wage workers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Singaporeans aged 40 to 60 in 2020 received a $500 top-up that was similar in intent.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will merge any remaining balance with this new mid-career top-up and the balance will likewise no longer expire at the end of 2025.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For those who wish to pursue another full-time diploma, we will now provide additional subsidies to do so.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Currently, Singaporeans can only receive one bout of Government subsidies for a full-time diploma at polytechnics, ITE and the arts institutions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Going back to the ITE-upgrader in the chart as an example, if he wants to pursue a career in a new sector like the digital economy, he can pursue a full-time SkillsFuture Career Transition programme.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: SSG provides approximately $10,000 in subsidies for the training and the remaining course fees will be fully offset by the $4,000 SkillsFuture Credit.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: He can also pursue a second full-time diploma in a high-growth area.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: He will receive subsidies of about $60,000 and his out-of-pocket course fees for the full-time diploma can also be partially offset by the $4,000 credit.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Using the ITE-upgrader in the chart as an example, the lifetime investment in education and skills could go up to as high as $380,000 in total.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is a substantial investment and commitment on the part of the Government.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we know that course fees are not the only constraint when it comes to upskilling.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Adult workers may have other financial commitments and concerns.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It could be difficult to take time off work to upskill and to lose income during the training period.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Hence, on top of our investment in educational programmes, we will provide a Training Allowance for Singaporeans aged 40 and above who pursue full-time IHL full qualifications or full-time SCTP.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Individuals, including self-employed persons and freelancers will receive the allowance as long as they have earned income based on Government's records in the latest available 12-month period.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Members have asked whether the long-term unemployed and caregivers who have left the workforce for some time will qualify for the training allowance.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At this point in time, they will not, as the allowance is meant to provide support for workers who experience income loss when they commit to full-time training.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, they can still make use of the $4,000 SkillsFuture Credit to refresh their skills through industry-relevant training.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They can also tap on career facilitation services and placement programmes that offer training allowance offered by Workforce Singapore and the National Trades Union Congress’ (NTUC's) Employment and Employability Institute.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Overall, the training allowance thresholds reflect our carefully considered approach.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The supported full-time courses are chosen to facilitate placement and entry into good jobs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The amount of support provides enough coverage for the median mid-career worker, while preserving the incentive to return to work.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The duration of support will cover more than one bout of full-time upgrading via SCTP and at least half the duration of a full qualification.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In total, our lifetime commitment to help an individual will be around $300,000 or higher, not counting the Training Allowance of up to $72,000.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: While the exact amount may differ for different paths, the concept is similar – continuous investments for the next 50 years beyond the school, rather than just the first 15 years in school.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will make available the full slide to all Members after the speech.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is a significant investment and commitment by the Government and it underscores our commitment to SkillsFuture as a key pillar of our social compact.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Members have asked more broadly, how do we measure the success of SkillsFuture?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The spending and course attendance numbers are just input and output indicators respectively.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The real outcomes we want to track are employment, wages and the competitiveness of our workers and enterprises.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is neither short term, nor a one-to-one causal relationship.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, reskilling may have helped workers keep their jobs or transit to new careers, beyond getting a pay rise.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Often, it also takes time for workers to cumulate and apply their newly acquired skills and for employers to see the tangible benefits of a higher skills base.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There are also other intangible benefits for our economy and society, which are important but are not easily measured, such as greater confidence for businesses to invest in Singapore, with our highly skilled and adaptable workforce.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Hence, the success of the SkillsFuture movement is about ultimately, whether Singaporeans have the confidence and competence to seize new career opportunities and tackle the future and whether our enterprises are well-positioned to capture new business opportunities because they have the quality of manpower required.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This vision of success cannot be achieved by the Government alone.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the spirit of Forward SG, we must journey together – IHLs, employers and individuals.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They are responding to industry needs to offer relevant courses and developing new programmes in emerging economic sectors.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The are refreshing their CET capabilities to meet the wide range of workforce needs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: More and more of our IHL capacities are shifting to support CET, beyond the conventional pre-employment training (PET).

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Employers, unions and enterprises will need to play their part too, to support workers with flexible working arrangements when they are upgrading, to work with employees to identify the new skills and competencies needed by the market and the companies, to recognise and remunerate employees based on those skills and competencies rather than just credentials and to create a culture of learning in every company, both small and medium enterprises, and large companies alike.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And every individual will need to take ownership of their individual path, to plan their directions and way forward and to have the courage and conviction to take their first step.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Government will do what we can to partner our people and industries to achieve this vision of us for SkillsFuture to be a key pillar of our social compact to keep our people competitive and employable over the long haul.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Next, let me touch on education as a celebration of our students' diverse strengths.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We must resist the temptation to "teach to the average" and instead focus on bringing out the best in every child.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have introduced Full Subject-based Banding, or Full SBB, for the Secondary 1 cohort this year.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are now overcoming the challenges of reorganising the classes and shuffling timetables to match the resources available.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But the positive outcomes in learning and social mixing give us confidence that this is the right thing to do, notwithstanding the challenges.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, I will touch on what students can expect at the end of their secondary school experience under the new system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, students take different examinations, with different provisions for different streams.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example. students in the previous Normal stream sit for "N" levels in September, while Express students sit for "O" levels in October. "O" level students have two examination sittings for their mother tongue language (MTL), one mid-year, one end-of-year, while "N" level students do not.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Under Full SBB, there will no longer be separate "N" or "O" level examination periods.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Instead, there will be one common SEC examination period, with different papers for different subject levels.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This means we will have one written SEC examination sitting for all MTL subject levels.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I understand that some may be concerned that they will have one less chance to improve their MTL grades.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we need to strike a careful balance between striving for excellence, chasing the last mark, and allowing our students to learn at a better pace.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When we introduced the mid-year "O" level MTL examination sitting in 1980, less than 40% of our students passed both their First and Second Languages.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, we allowed students to take their MTL examination twice, to meet the Second Language requirement for Pre-University.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, almost all our "O" level MTL students already meet the language requirement within their first sitting.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But most importantly, the new system will allow our students and teachers to better pace the MTL curriculum, with four more months of learning, rather than to squeeze everything into three-and-a-half years in preparation for the June examination sitting.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To spread out the examination load at the end of the year, students will sit for their English and MTL written examinations in the second week of September, one month ahead of other subjects.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: After taking their examinations, students will receive a common certificate, the SEC, which will replace the current "O", N(A) and N(T) level certificates.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The certificate will reflect each student's subject combinations and levels.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Just like the "A" level certificate, which reflects each student's subjects and the level they have completed at – H1, H2 or H3.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The certificate will continue to be jointly awarded by MOE and Cambridge, to preserve its standing.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The SEC will allow students offering a mix of subject levels to access a wider range of post-secondary pathways.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For students applying to Polytechnic Year 1, admission today is based on an "ELR2B2", otherwise known as English, Relevant to and the Best Two aggregate score comprising five "O" levels, or G3 subjects.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second Minister Dr Mohamad Maliki Osman will provide more details.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: From time to time, some call for MOE to remove examinations like the PSLE.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Others ask us to bring back mid-year examinations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, let me state that if we see our worth as being defined by examination results only, removing PSLE will not remove stress.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Instead, we need to help our students manage and overcome stress.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We need to understand that examinations like the PSLE and SEC are not an end in themselves, but they are means to help our children find a suitable learning environment in the next stage of their learning journey.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As I have mentioned before, there are non-trivial issues to overcome for a through-train concept, such as, how will we select students who are suitable for which school at age six?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we cannot select, how will we support diverse learning profiles for the next 10 years for us to be able to stretch the high ability students, while supporting those with higher needs?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We may end up "teaching to the average", which does not bring out the best in any child.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And this will make teaching even more challenging for our already stretched teachers to cater to a class with such diverse abilities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we allow transfers out of the school, then, the question is: who gets to be posted out and to where?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Will the stronger students try to transfer out, leaving the through-train as an option for the weaker students only?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Or if it is the weaker students that leave, then school assessments might become the new frontier of stress, as students worry about performing well enough to remain in the said school.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And which school will take these students to integrate them back into the mainstream curriculum and at what point in time?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, MOE is considering it but let us be upfront about these proposals.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They are not without merits, but certainly they come with tradeoffs and non-trivial implications.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Let us make help our students to understand their strengths in the meantime, approach stress and challenges with the right mindset and use exams to right-site themselves for the next stage of learning, rather than as a competition to beat others.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In fact, we know that good grades are not enough to prepare our students for the future.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, the EAGLES and Edusave Skills Award are given to students who have excelled in non-academic activities or who have demonstrated leadership qualities and served the community.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will increase the number of these awards to recognise 21CC and LifeSkills.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Younger students will receive the award if they demonstrate attributes like creativity in generating ideas to solve problems in their school or outside while older students in polytechnics and ITE might demonstrate interpersonal and collaboration skills by working effectively with their colleagues in an internship.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This signals our commitment to reducing the overemphasis on academic results and balancing that with better preparation more holistically for the future.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our efforts to celebrate diverse strengths must also extend to students with SEN.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: One key challenge for the families of children with disabilities are the significant out-of-pocket expenses.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But beyond financial support, I also want to share my vision for the SPED sector, which has been close to my heart since my Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF) days.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I want our young people to aspire to join SPED fraternity, be inspired by its deep sense of mission, like any mainstream teacher.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I want our SPED educators to have promising careers, that will encourage them to stay in the sector, like the mainstream.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I want our SPED school leaders to have structured and rigorous leadership development opportunities, like the mainstream.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I want our SPED sector to have their own communities of practice, specialising and developing deep authoritative professional body of knowledge for each of the SPED specialisation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I want mainstream and SPED educators to grow together, with porosity of pathways, sharing best practices and supporting each other.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I want to see the SPED students having pathways integrated with their post-18 work, life and care arrangements.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Chair, recently, I met the leaders of our 25 SPED schools.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I want to say that after the meeting, it is no longer my vision.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I want to thank all the SPED school leaders for agreeing to work together, towards our shared vision for the sector.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We agreed we are not where we want to be, not yet.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we know where we want to get to and we are determined to get there for the sake of our children.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second Minister Dr Mohamad Maliki Osman will share more details about our efforts.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Now, let me turn to the third point.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Education must be a collective effort from all of society.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This leads me to how we must fundamentally reshape the way we see education.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Education must be a collective effort from all of society.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, I want to thank two groups of people for their contributions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, our Parent Support Groups, which have stepped up to support our students' well-being and development.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Minister of State Gan Siow Huang will be sharing an update in her speech of how we have expanded the Parent Support Groups and how we have strengthened their capabilities to partner our school.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But above all, I want to recognise our educators.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: More than any policy change, it is our teachers who are key to preparing our students for the future.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We recognise the challenges that our teachers face and we will continue to support them, through what I call three "T"s.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, our Language Feedback Assistant for English provides feedback for basic language errors in students' writing.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This allows our teachers to spend more of their time guiding students on higher-order elements, such as logic and persuasiveness and creates time for teachers to work with students in the same class who require more attention or support.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: What we recognise is that it is not always easy to use new technologies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It takes time for us to feel at ease with them and trust them to complement our work.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, many of us may have struggled in the early days of COVID-19 in shifting our work online.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, I want to salute our teachers who are challenging themselves to adapt to these new tools, not just because they are new and exciting, but because they will help our students learn better and relieve the load of our teachers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second T is linked to technology, but the second T is time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Technology will not replace our teachers, but it will change their roles and responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our teachers will spend less time, going forward, delivering information and more time facilitating learning and collaboration.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They will spend less time delivering information as information becomes commoditised, but they will spend more time facilitating learning and collaboration, which are higher order skills.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our teachers undergo years of rigorous training and professional development.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They are experts in their subject areas and pedagogy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They invest their time and energy to nurture our students, often going above and beyond their official responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, we ask that everyone respect and trust our teachers to do their work as professionals and to support them in giving the best opportunities to our students to develop their talents, find their footing and understand their strengths and weaknesses.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But change is not easy, especially if we are to reshape our own perspective and redefine our definitions of success.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But change will be impossible if we do not try.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But if we can come together to refresh our understanding of education and what it means for all of us, it can underscore Singapore's success for the next 50 years and beyond.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Chairman, lifelong learning and SkillsFuture Level-Up seems to be the buzzword.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Many Members of Parliament (MPs), including myself, have spoken about it.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I highlighted that amid all this excitement, there are potential stresses and anxieties surrounding career transitions or just returning back to school after so many years.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, some clarity is needed as well as increased support in their endeavours.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Additionally, would the Ministry consider introducing more tailored financial support schemes to reduce the financial and emotional burden on individuals pursuing their studies?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Next, would the Ministry consider developing flexible and innovative learning pathways for a more inclusive approach for education as well as training?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: By offering part-time and innovative modular courses, we can cater to a mature learner's diverse needs and schedules, some of whom are parents and caregivers.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This can reduce the pressure of a full-time commitment and facilitate a smoother integration of learning into their daily lives.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Lastly, would the Ministry consider establishing a comprehensive support system encompassing career guidance, like what we see for our secondary school students, mental health resources and networking opportunities that would aid in the professional development of our mature workforce and support their mental and emotional well-being throughout this journey?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: I welcome the initiatives announced by the Ministry last week and the Minister's remarks about education as a continuing journey.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Lifelong learning is a powerful tool for promoting social mobility, creating positive change within our communities and unlocking opportunities for everyone to thrive and contribute meaningfully to society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: SkillsFuture is an initiative that facilitates and promotes both lifelong learning and Singapore's growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: What programmes are in place to encourage employers to approve leave for employees wanting to participate in the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme, ensure that those who graduate from such programmes are able to secure employment in the area of their study, and mentor those wanting to participate in such programme to ensure that they are making an informed career choice?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Lifelong learning within the education system goes beyond imparting knowledge.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is about equipping children with the skills, confidence and curiosity to become lifelong learners who are motivated to pursue their aspirations and reach their full potential.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In view of this, my questions are: what programmes are in place to introduce the concept of lifelong learning into early childhood education and care settings, and what programmes are in place to encourage school-aged children to explore and adopt a philosophy of lifelong learning?

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, parents play a fundamental role in nurturing lifelong learning in their children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Providing the foundation, support and encouragement needed for them to become curious, motivated and self-directed learners throughout their lives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In view of this, my questions are: what programmes are in place to assist parents to discuss the concept of lifelong learning with their children at home, and what programmes are in place to encourage parents to actively support their children to pursue life choices, including academic and vocational choices, based on personal interest or aptitude rather than social or cultural expectations or norms?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Chairman, Forward Singapore's Equip pillar sets out how education and learning can equip Singaporeans with the knowledge and skills to seize new opportunities and maximise their potential.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Minister Chan Chun Sing shared last week more details on the subsidies for Singaporeans aged 40 and above to pursue another full-time diploma at the local polytechnic.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: It is not easy for someone well-past the conventional graduation age of early 20s to go back to full-time studies.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Mature students are likely to have financial commitments to support their families.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: They could already be parents and may also have to take care of their own elderly parents' financial commitments.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Would this act against them in their eligibility for the training allowance?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: As the term lifelong learning goes, learning does not stop in the early 20s after graduation nor does it restart at 40 years old.

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: Are there support provisions for Singaporeans aged under 40 years old?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: How about Singaporeans who want to go further than a second full-time diploma?

speaker: Mr Baey Yam Keng (Tampines)
text: What support could be made available for those whose career paths and aspirations would benefit more from a second degree programme?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, the Government's commitment to lifelong learning, SkillsFuture and SkillsFuture Level-Up is crucial for propelling Singaporeans up the value chain, garnering support from employers.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Such specialised training is deemed essential for building a talent pool with the advanced skills necessary to achieve the Manufacturing 2030 vision.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As the job landscape evolves rapidly, recognising workplaces as extensions of our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) could enable a more practice-based and application-oriented approach to human capital development.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Trade associations and chambers (TACs) may have a part to play in overseeing and accrediting workplace training, and this adjustment could ensure that the workforce remains agile and employable in the face of changing industrial requirements.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As such, will the Ministry of Education (MOE) consider expanding SkillsFuture support to include various forms of workplace training?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, for myself and many in this Chamber, one of the most striking announcements in Budget 2024 is the significant investment the Government is making to support lifelong learning, upskilling and reskilling.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, these are significant investments and it will be important to demonstrate the impact and value of these investments over time.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Indeed, beyond the direct investments in the course fee subsidies and training allowances, significant effort will need to be made to curate the right courses, raise awareness, help people overcome the mental, physical and financial hurdles to take ownership of their learning, match them to the right courses and use the newly-acquired knowledge and skills to land a job or move up in their current roles with better salaries and prospects.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We also need to make sure that people are resilient and adopt a never-give-up attitude, both in learning and in looking for jobs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How will the Government ensure that this significant investment will achieve the desired results, in particular, of helping Singaporeans grow in their careers and take on new careers?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This is particularly important to ensure that we have SkillsFuture programmes designed specially to target skills upgrading and acquisition, rather than to achieve academic qualifications.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: By drawing lessons from similar setups in Sweden and Switzerland, these specialised training providers ought to be established with the following criteria.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: First, there must be assurance that training delivered is highly applied and practice-based, with clear reference to industry skills-maps.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This approach ensures that the learners acquire practical skills and hands-on experience, making them job-ready upon completion of their courses.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Second, it is essential for instructors and trainings to have strong industry experience.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Educators with an industry background bring a wealth of knowledge, real-world insights and practical skills to the classroom.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The teaching pedagogy for adult learners must be contextualised within the industry landscape, leveraging real-world case studies and use cases.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Third, the credentials awarded upon training completion must translate into industry-recognised and valued qualifications, rather than merely reflecting academic grades.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The learners should receive credentials that will demonstrate their ability to apply learned skills in real-world settings recognised and importantly, endorsed by employers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Fourth, the active participation of employers in the training design ensures direct relevance to industry requirements and that training is rooted in real-world applications than in theory.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They should be involved in the identification and prioritising of training programmes that will address the most sought-after skills and competencies in the job market.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The endorsement and commitment of employers to adopt these training programmes must be an integral part of the design and funding process of SkillsFuture.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In countries like Sweden and Switzerland, industry-specialised schools are often led and governed by industry leaders, exemplifying this approach.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, to establish an ecosystem of training providers that will yield high employment outcomes, it is necessary to pivot SkillsFuture to support industry-linked training providers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These industry-linked training providers must be deeply integrated with the sectors they serve.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Forming partnerships with the industry and employers is crucial to ensure their curricula are directly informed by current and future skills needs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The course offerings should undergo regular review cycles to remain responsive to evolving industry trends and skills demands.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Additionally, the assessment of learning outcomes must align with industry relevance rather than concentrating on academic rigour, the assessment should prioritise skills acquisition and the performance of relevant skills and tasks in real world settings.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Furthermore, it is imperative that industry leaders have a strong representation on the board of directors of these schools to ensure strong alignment of the schools' resources and outcomes to industry needs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Implementing such a measure would foster the evolution of a new generation of highly specialised schools, each with deep domain expertise in their respective industries.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Knowing that their time invested in training has a real impact on boosting business performance and career growth will be a key driver for participation and commitment.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Chairman, freelancers I spoke with welcomed the new SkillsFuture Level-Up programme.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They include platform workers who appreciate the Government's consideration of their challenges faced when exploring career transition.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Some, such as Miss R, a freelance delivery courier and an Institute of Technical Education (ITE) graduate, asked if the Government could consider extending the SkillsFuture Level-Up programme and/or the ITE Progression Award to her and her peers in their 30s.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: She turned to food delivery after she was displaced some years ago.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Then, she had found it challenging to upgrade her qualification as she had breadwinner responsibilities.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Now, as she contemplates her career options against the backdrop of economic uncertainty and an appreciation of CPF utility for ageing, health and housing needs, she hopes that the sandwiched group of ITE graduates, like her, can also be considered for the ITE Progression Award and/or the SkillsFuture Level-Up Programme.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, I would like to put forth three possibilities for the Minister's consideration.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Second, might the Ministry and SkillsFuture Singapore (SSG) work closely with the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) and its freelancer-centred associations to include, under the SkillsFuture Level-Up programme, training options and accreditations that are helpful to progressing the work prospects of those who are dictated by business models in the arts, creative, media and coaching sectors to freelance as a career?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Third, might the Ministry and SSG work closely with NTUC and its freelancer-centred associations as well as relevant sector agencies to establish fair and balanced guidance that communicate the surveyed costs for freelancers, such as coaches and creatives, to deliver quality service of professional standards?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: These professional standards could be benchmarked against occupation-specific competency frameworks that were outlined in the Ministry of Manpower's (MOM's) 2018 Tripartite Workgroup report on support for self-employed persons.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The guidance would also recognise the differentiated premiums for expertise mastery that freelancers, like coaches and creatives, accumulate through upskilling efforts.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: By contextualising initiatives, we can take concrete steps together to boost freelancers' career prospects and their value-add to the Singapore economy.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Skills relevant to the latter group might not be directly related to "employability".

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, freelancers and SEPs may benefit more from training in targeted areas, such as the negotiation of contract terms, business and accounting management and product marketing.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Undoubtedly, these skills may be valued by prospective employers as well, but I would like to seek clarification from the Ministry on how SkillsFuture Level-Up courses will take the specific learning needs of freelancers into account.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister has stated that the long-term unemployed and caregivers who have left the workforce will not be entitled to the allowance, as it is meant to provide support for workers and, specifically, those who experience income loss when they commit to full-time training.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The benefit, therefore, for now, excludes people, such as caregivers who have had to take time off from paid work in order to look after children or the elderly, and it appears to gloss over the fact that caregiving is also a kind of work.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It is just unpaid and outside the formal confines of an employer-employee relationship.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If the Government wishes for seniors to be able to age in place and for more women to bear children, there must be recognition of the fact that time-consuming and all-encompassing caregiving duties will necessarily be borne by Singaporeans and, most typically, by women.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that the Government can consider an eventual extension of the training allowance to caregivers if they wish to upskill themselves with a view to re-entering the workforce when their caregiving duties have ceased or when they become less onerous.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
